In the repo at /Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/soph-sec-redact (a Go CLI that captures AI agent transcripts), I need an inventory of JSON key names that actually appear in real agent transcript fixtures/testdata, for these three families. Search testdata directories, *_test.go fixture strings, e2e fixtures, and any .jsonl/.json fixture files. Be very thorough.

1. Keys ending in "id" or "ids" (case-insensitively). I need the EXACT spellings as they appear, e.g. `id`, `uuid`, `session_id`, `sessionId`, `tool_use_id`, `toolUseId`, `parentUuid`, `leafUuid`, `sid`, `uid`, `pid`, `cid`, `guid`, `request_id`, `message_id`, `ids`, `fileIds`, etc. Also report any key ending in those letters that is NOT an identifier (e.g. `valid`, `invalid`, `android`, `hybrid`, `grid`, `solid`, `candid`, `overrid...`).

2. Keys ending in "signature" (case-insensitively) — exact spellings, e.g. `signature`, `thinkingSignature`, `x_signature`.

3. Objects with a `type` field whose value starts with "image" or equals "base64" — report the exact `type` values seen and the surrounding object shape (which keys hold the payload: `data`, `source`, `source.data`, `image_url.url`, `media_type`, etc.). Also report any `type` value that starts with "image" but is NOT an image payload.

Also: report the exact spellings of any path-like keys seen (`path`, `file_path`, `filePath`, `cwd`, `root`, `dir`, `directory`, `notebook_path`, etc.) and a few REAL example values for each.

Report findings as lists with file:line citations for the notable ones. Do not modify any files.

Metrics datasets follow different rules from trace/event datasets — many operations (bare COUNT, RATE_SUM, RATE_AVG, RATE_MAX, CONCURRENCY) are forbidden, temporal aggregation is automatic, and each metric has its own attributes. Use this skill when querying a metrics dataset (gauges, counters, histograms, sums), asking about temporal aggregation (RATE, INCREASE, SUMMARIZE, LAST), finding the metrics dataset or discovering metric names and attributes, debugging unexpected metrics query results, or querying infrastructure metrics like CPU, memory, disk I/O, or network stats. Do NOT use for instrumenting metrics (use otel-instrumentation), querying event datasets with "metrics" in their name, or conceptual questions (use observability-fundamentals).
